The trick is to treat your kitchen lighting like a DC power distribution network rather than a series of fixed lamps. To achieve that "ballast" level of brightness with the modularity of a children’s toy, I recommend the following architecture:

1. The "Ballast" Light Source: 24V COB LEDs

For high-output lighting that looks integrated, use High-Density 24V COB LED strips (at least 480 LEDs/m).

  • Brightness: These can output over 1,200 lumens per meter. Running them at 60–70% via a PWM dimmer will keep them cool, extend their lifespan, and still be significantly brighter than the IKEA bars.
  • Voltage: 24V is superior for modularity because it suffers far less "voltage drop" over longer wire runs, allowing you to daisy-chain or branch out more easily.

2. The "Snap-and-Play" Hardware

To get that "alligator clip" or "toy-like" ease of installation without the fire hazard, use a combination of these three components:

ComponentFunctionThe "Snap" Factor
Wago 221 Lever-NutsMain Hubs / BranchingTool-free. You just lift the orange lever, insert a stripped wire, and snap it shut. It's the most reliable way to create a "bus" for your power distribution.
JST-SM or XT30 ConnectorsModular Light BarsCrimp these onto the ends of your LED segments. They provide a satisfying "click" and allow you to swap or move light bars in seconds. XT30s (used in drones) are overkill but feel incredibly "pro."
3D-Printed Snap MountsMounting & Cable ManagementUse a Bambu Lab A1 to print custom clips that snap onto your aluminum channels. You can design them with integrated cable stays to keep the wiring tucked away.

3. Proposed Modular Setup

Instead of buying a $30 bar, you can build a custom one for roughly $8–$12 using this workflow:

  1. The Channel: Buy bulk 1-meter aluminum U-channels. Cut them to your exact cabinet widths.
  2. The Strip: Adhere your COB LED strip inside.
  3. The Interface: Solder a JST-SM female pigtail to the end of the strip.
  4. The Distribution: Run a "trunk line" of 18/2 AWG wire under your cabinets. Every few feet, use a 3-port Wago 221 to tap into that trunk and provide a JST-SM male pigtail.

Pro Tip: If you want true "alligator clip" levels of modularity, you can look into Magnetic Pogo Pin connectors. They allow the light bars to simply "snap" onto a powered track using magnets, but they require a bit more DIY precision to align.

Why this beats retail:

  • Cost: You can buy a 5-meter roll of high-end COB LEDs for ~$30. That’s five 3-foot bars for the price of one IKEA bar.
  • Repairability: If one segment fails or you decide you want a different color temperature, you just unplug the JST connector and swap the bar. No need to rip out the entire wiring harness.
  • The "Dimming" Sweet Spot: By over-speccing the brightness and running at 70%, you avoid the "angry blue" flicker of cheap LEDs and get a warm, high-quality glow that feels much more expensive than it is.

The "Standard Unit" Specification

Instead of custom-cutting to your cabinets, build a fleet of two standard sizes. These will fit 90% of all cabinetry layouts globally.

  • Unit A (The "Short"): 12 inches (30 cm)
  • Unit B (The "Long"): 24 inches (60 cm)

Each unit will consist of an aluminum channel, a COB strip, and a 5.5mm x 2.1mm DC Barrel Jack pigtail hanging off the end. This is the "Gold Standard" for low-voltage DIY; it's robust, cheap, and allows you to "plug and play" just like a consumer product.

The "Snap-and-Play" Wiring Architecture

To keep this modular and reusable for your next home, do not hard-wire the lights to each other. Instead, use a Star Topology:

  1. The Power Hub: Place your 24V transformer in a central location (e.g., above the microwave or in a corner cabinet).
  2. The Distribution Bus: Run two main wires (positive/negative) from the transformer into a 5-port Wago 221 Lever-Nut. This is now your "Power Strip."
  3. The Modular Leads: From that Wago hub, run individual wires to each cabinet section. Terminate each wire with a Female DC Barrel Jack.
  4. The Light Bar: Your DIY light bars will have a Male DC Barrel Jack.

The Result: You simply "snap" the bar under the cabinet and "plug" it into the waiting jack. If you move, you unplug the bars, snap open the Wago levers to reclaim your wire, and pack it all in a box.

Implementation Notes for "Ballast" Brightness

  • Over-Spec the Density: Buy strips rated for 15W to 20W per meter. At 100% brightness, this will be blinding—excellent for a "ballast" feel.
  • Voltage Choice: Stick strictly to 24V. If you use 12V and try to run them at high brightness over a modular "plug" system, you will encounter significant heat and voltage drop (dimming at the end of the line). 24V remains crisp and cool.
  • Affordability: Buying the 5-meter COB reel and bulk aluminum channels will bring your cost per "Standard Unit" down to approximately $7 to $11, significantly beating the $30 IKEA alternative while offering triple the light output.
